outputs.L1:
In the present paper, we propose an apparently new method for finding closed-form solutions to certain types of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). The method is based on decomposing nonlinear operators into sequences of lower-order operators. We show that this decomposition can be performed through an iterative procedure, with each step reduced to solving an auxiliary system of PDEs for a single dependent variable. In this process, we also derive explicit first-order PDEs for the first integrals of the decomposable initial PDEs. Remarkably, these first-order PDEs are linear when the initial PDE is linear in its highest-order derivatives.

The proposed method has been implemented as a Maple procedure capable of solving a wide range of PDEs of different orders and with varying numbers of independent variables. Examples of PDEs for which general solutions are calculated demonstrate the method’s potential for the automated solution of nonlinear PDEs.
outputs.L2:
This paper introduces an apparently novel approach for obtaining closed-form solutions to certain classes of nonlinear partial differential equations. The approach factors nonlinear differential operators into sequences of lower-order operators. This factorization can be carried out iteratively, with each stage requiring the solution of one or more auxiliary PDE systems involving a single dependent variable. The procedure also yields explicit first-order PDEs whose solutions provide first integrals of the original decomposable equation. Notably, these first-order equations are linear whenever the original PDE depends linearly on its highest-order derivatives.

The method has been implemented as a Maple procedure capable of solving a wide range of PDEs with varying orders and numbers of independent variables. Examples in which general solutions are computed illustrate the method’s potential for the automated solution of nonlinear PDEs.
outputs.L3:
The paper introduces a new method for obtaining closed-form solutions to a broad class of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). The central idea is to decompose a nonlinear differential operator into a sequence of lower-order operators using an iterative procedure. By reducing the order and complexity of the original equation step by step, the method provides a systematic framework for identifying first integrals and constructing explicit solutions.

At each stage of the iteration, the approach requires solving auxiliary systems of PDEs involving a single dependent variable. These systems determine the coefficients and functions needed for the operator decomposition. An important feature of the method is that it produces explicit first-order PDEs whose solutions yield first integrals of the original equation. Moreover, when the original PDE is linear in its highest-order derivatives, the resulting equations for the first integrals are themselves linear, making them more tractable with standard analytical or symbolic techniques.

The authors also implement the procedure in Maple to assess its computational feasibility. The implementation successfully handles PDEs of different orders and with varying numbers of independent variables. These results demonstrate the method’s versatility and suggest that it could form the basis of an automated symbolic framework for solving nonlinear PDEs and deriving closed-form solutions.
outputs.L4:
A new closed-form approach is presented for solving a broad class of nonlinear partial differential equations. The method is based on an iterative decomposition of the original nonlinear differential operator into operators of progressively lower order. At each stage, an auxiliary system of partial differential equations is constructed and solved for a single dependent variable. The resulting expression is then used to derive a first-order PDE whose solutions provide first integrals of the original equation. Repeating this reduction can transform a difficult higher-order nonlinear problem into a sequence of simpler equations that are more amenable to symbolic treatment.

An important feature of the approach is that the final first-order PDE becomes linear whenever the original equation is linear with respect to its highest-order derivatives, even if lower-order terms remain nonlinear. This property substantially simplifies the search for first integrals and makes the method particularly suitable for computer-algebra implementation. Once the required first integrals have been identified, they can be used to reduce the order of the PDE or, in favorable cases, to construct its solution in closed form.

The procedure has been implemented in Maple and tested on a diverse collection of partial differential equations. These examples include equations with different orders, nonlinear structures, and combinations of dependent and independent variables. The implementation successfully obtains closed-form results in cases that can be difficult to handle using standard symbolic techniques. The experiments therefore indicate that iterative operator decomposition offers a systematic and effective framework for automating the solution of nonlinear PDEs, while also providing a promising foundation for further development of computer-algebra tools in this area.

**Partial Differential Equations**

PDEs, or partial differential equations, are mathematical equations that describe how quantities change across space and time. The equations are widely used to model phenomena such as heat transfer, fluid flow, electromagnetic fields, and wave propagation. Unlike ordinary differential equations, PDEs involve derivatives with respect to two or more independent variables. Moreover, they provide essential tools for understanding complex systems in physics, engineering, biology, and finance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper proposing a new method for finding closed-form solutions of nonlinear partial differential equations by decomposing nonlinear operators into lower-order operators, including a Maple implementation and examples.
counterfactuals.output: We propose a symbolic method for constructing closed-form solutions of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) by decomposing nonlinear differential operators into compositions of lower-order operators. The approach converts a given nonlinear PDE into a system of simpler differential constraints whose compatibility conditions determine admissible factorizations and solution families. This reduction facilitates the identification of exact solutions that may be difficult to obtain using standard ansatz-based, symmetry, or direct integration techniques. An algorithmic formulation of the method is presented, together with a Maple implementation that automates operator decomposition, coefficient matching, compatibility analysis, and symbolic verification of the resulting solutions. The effectiveness of the procedure is illustrated through representative nonlinear PDEs, including equations with polynomial and nonpolynomial nonlinearities. The examples demonstrate that the proposed framework can recover known solutions and generate additional closed-form solutions under explicit parameter conditions. The method provides a systematic and computationally accessible tool for the exact analysis of nonlinear PDEs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise academic abstract about an iterative PDE decomposition technique in which each step requires solving auxiliary systems for one dependent variable. Mention first integrals and automated symbolic computation.
counterfactuals.output: We present an iterative decomposition technique for systems of partial differential equations in which each stage reduces the original problem to auxiliary systems involving a single dependent variable. First integrals of these auxiliary systems generate successive reductions and reveal structural relations among the equations. The method is well suited to automated symbolic computation, enabling systematic derivation, compatibility testing, and reconstruction of solutions. This framework provides an effective approach to simplifying nonlinear PDE systems and identifying exact solution structures.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Please generate a paper abstract describing a method for factoring higher-order nonlinear PDE operators, deriving first-order PDEs for their first integrals, and showing that these equations are linear when the original PDE is linear in its highest derivatives.
counterfactuals.output: We present a systematic method for factoring higher-order nonlinear partial differential operators and constructing associated first integrals. The approach represents a differential operator of order \(m\) through compositions of lower-order, principally first-order, operators, with the factorization conditions obtained by matching coefficients on the appropriate jet space. Each admissible factor determines a first integral whose level sets reduce the original equation to a first-order PDE. We derive explicit determining equations for these integrals by requiring compatibility between the candidate first-order relation and the original higher-order PDE under total differentiation. Although the determining equations are generally nonlinear, we show that they become linear in the unknown first integral and its derivatives whenever the original PDE depends linearly—though not necessarily homogeneously—on its highest-order derivatives. This establishes a direct connection between quasilinearity at the highest differential order and the tractability of the first-integral construction. The framework provides an algorithmic route to order reduction, factorization, and solution generation for broad classes of nonlinear PDEs, while recovering familiar operator factorizations in the fully linear case.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a mathematical study that develops and implements in Maple an algorithm for solving nonlinear PDEs of varying orders and numbers of independent variables through operator decomposition. Emphasize closed-form general solutions and illustrative examples.
counterfactuals.output:
The study presents a symbolic algorithm, implemented in Maple, for solving nonlinear partial differential equations with different orders and arbitrary numbers of independent variables. Its central idea is to decompose the PDE into differential operators, isolate a conveniently invertible operator, and repeatedly apply its inverse. The resulting recursive relations generate the solution components while preserving the integration data—arbitrary constants or functions—needed to obtain a general solution rather than only a particular one.

The Maple implementation automates the operator decomposition, symbolic integrations, nonlinear substitutions, and simplification of the resulting series. When the recursive expansion terminates or can be summed, the method produces an exact closed-form general solution, including the appropriate arbitrary functions associated with the PDE’s order.

A range of illustrative examples—covering nonlinear equations of various orders and involving different numbers of independent variables—shows how the procedure works in practice. These examples demonstrate that the algorithm can recover compact exact solutions, handle nonlinear terms systematically, and provide a unified computer-algebra framework for classes of PDEs that would otherwise require separate, problem-specific techniques.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an abstract, in the style of a non-native English-speaking mathematics researcher, for a paper on automatic solution of decomposable nonlinear PDEs using iterative lower-order operator decomposition and auxiliary PDE systems.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** In this paper, an automatic method is proposed for solving a class of decomposable nonlinear partial differential equations. The main idea is to represent a given higher-order nonlinear differential operator by an iterative composition of lower-order operators. At every decomposition step, an auxiliary system of PDEs is constructed, whose compatibility conditions characterize admissible intermediate variables and decomposition parameters. In this way, the solution of the original equation is reduced to successive solution of lower-order equations, which are usually more convenient for symbolic and numerical treatment. An algorithm is presented for detecting possible decompositions, generating the corresponding auxiliary PDE systems, and verifying the obtained solutions by substitution into the initial equation. The method can also distinguish complete, conditional, and approximate decompositions. Several examples for nonlinear equations of second and higher orders are considered to demonstrate the procedure. The obtained results show that iterative operator decomposition gives a useful framework for computer-assisted investigation of nonlinear PDEs and can produce exact solutions which are difficult to derive by direct methods.
